choices.value: The rate at which the radius changes as the volume changes
The rate at which the radius changes as the surface area changes

examples.knowledge_point: Interpreting the Derivative of a Function
examples.problem:
Consider a spherical balloon with radius $r.$ As the balloon loses air, its volume $V$ decreases. What is the best interpretation of $V'(r)?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13930198/assets/7f52288ca4670375413ecd5283bc2d15fbb332af311ead07986c1526d25e338a.png)
examples.worked_solution:
The function $V(r)$ gives the volume of a sphere with radius $r.$ So

$$
V'(r) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}V}{\textrm{d}r} = \dfrac{\textrm{Change in }V}{\textrm{Change in }r}.
$$

Therefore, $V'(r)$ is the rate at which the volume changes as the radius changes.

feedback.problem: A dairy farm sells milk on a particular day for $p(v)$ dollars, where $v$ is the number of liters of milk in the dairy farm at the start of the day. What are the units of $\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}v}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
We have that the price $p(v)$ is measured in dollars and the volume of milk is measured in liters. 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(v): & \text{dollars} \\ v: & \text{liters}\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative $\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}v}$ measures a change in $p(v)$ over a change in $v.$ So, it represents a ratio of the units:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}v}: & \frac{\text{dollars}}{\text{liters}}\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, $\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}v}$ is measured in "dollars per liter".
